what_this_is: Reviewed static explanatory metadata for the Workbench Project Map. It is the PLAIN-LANGUAGE layer only: it explains what things mean for a reader who does not write code. It is NOT an authority. It records no status, no ordering, no classification and no decision, and tools/state/project_intelligence.py never derives a status, a phase, a queue classification or an architectural relationship from anything in this file.
how_it_is_used: Every entry here is matched by key (a term, a capability id, a file path, a discovery id, a queue item_num) against elements the read model found in the live spine or on disk. A key present here but absent from the live state is reported as a stale vocabulary entry, never rendered as if the thing existed. A live element with no entry here is rendered with its technical text and the sentence 'Plain-language explanation not yet recorded.' Nothing in this file is generated by a model at page-load time; it is written and reviewed in the repository, and changing it is a reviewed commit.
authored: 2026-10-02, Workbench Project Map card. Grounded in the decision rows, project_state rows and dev_continuity_events summaries quoted by the read model beside each entry.

glossary.plain_english: A bundle of web routes that can be plugged into the live application.
glossary.technical_note: A Flask Blueprint. Code in a blueprint exists but does nothing until runtime/container_app.py registers it; registration is what makes its URLs answer.

glossary.plain_english: Code that organizes existing information for display without changing it.
glossary.technical_note: A module under tools/state/ that opens the database read-only, assembles one normalized answer, and writes nothing back.
A numbered .sql file under runtime/schema/migrations/. Applying one adds tables or columns. A migration being available is not the same as a feature being switched on.

glossary.plain_english: A web address the frontend uses to ask the backend for information or an allowed action.
glossary.technical_note: An HTTP route, for example GET /api/workbench/build-path.

glossary.plain_english: An independent reviewer checked the actual pushed GitHub code.
glossary.technical_note: A checkpoint state in project_state.external_dev_checkpoint, governed by ADR-XDEV-001. A SHA that has been pushed is not yet a SHA that has been accepted.

glossary.plain_english: The project's single memory file — the database that holds decisions, state, work items and findings.
glossary.technical_note: data/cis_memory.db, a SQLite database. Every read model on this screen opens it read-only.

glossary.plain_english: One recorded piece of work, with a number like 1.23.
glossary.technical_note: A row in the queue_items table. ADR-PIPE-006 makes queue_items + queue_edges the work-item authority, separate from the roadmap.

glossary.plain_english: Something true that was found during the work and written down so it cannot be quietly forgotten.
glossary.technical_note: A dev_continuity_events row of kind 'unfinished_work', carrying a disposition: RESOLVED_NOW, BEFORE_STAGE_CLOSEOUT or EXPLICITLY_DEFERRED.

glossary.plain_english: Going through the recorded work items and labelling each one, so the list can be understood and ordered.
glossary.technical_note: The bounded mechanical classification step ADR-PIPE-006 sequences after P0 and before P1. It has not happened yet.

glossary.plain_english: One step in the current build order.
glossary.technical_note: A stage in project_state.pipeline_roadmap, governed by ADR-PIPE-001. Phases are chronological; destination architecture nodes are not.

glossary.plain_english: Where a statement came from, so you can check it yourself.
glossary.technical_note: On this screen every relationship carries authority_refs naming the decision id, state key or database row it was read from.

glossary.plain_english: A written decision the project has to keep to.
glossary.technical_note: Architecture Decision Record. A row in project_decisions, for example ADR-PIPE-001.

glossary.plain_english: Something the system can actually do for you, like signing in or holding a conversation.
glossary.technical_note: On this screen a capability is a DERIVED read-model grouping, not a stored authority. CIS has no capability table; see the capability provenance note.
ADR-PIPE-005's BUILT_BUT_DORMANT: the implementation exists in the repository, its blueprint is not registered, and its migration is not applied.

glossary.plain_english: A way of writing a diagram as text so the picture is generated from the same data as the words beside it.
glossary.technical_note: Diagram source generated server-side by the read model, laid out in the browser by MermaidDiagram.jsx.

glossary.plain_english: The layer underneath that everything else is built on top of.
glossary.technical_note: ADR-WIASW-002 records CIS as the generalized deterministic AI and control substrate underneath WIASW.

areas.label: Overview
areas.plain_question: How do the parts of this map fit together?
areas.plain_english: A starting point. It shows the five other views, the headline numbers behind each, and how a problem connects through to the thing it is eventually meant to support.

areas.label: Current Build
areas.plain_english: The P0 to P6 sequence the project is actually working through, where it currently is, and what is holding it up. This view is the existing Build Path screen, not a second copy of it.

areas.label: Queue / Problems
areas.plain_question: What work and unresolved problems exist?
areas.plain_english: Two different lists kept apart. Problems are findings written down during the work. Queue items are recorded pieces of work. Most queue items have not been labelled yet, and this view shows that rather than guessing the labels.

areas.label: System Anatomy
areas.plain_english: The major working parts of CIS, what each one is for, whether it is switched on, and which files implement it.

areas.label: Destination
areas.plain_question: What are we ultimately building toward?
areas.plain_english: WIASW — the product architecture CIS is being built to support. None of it is activated work. This view is the existing Destination Architecture screen, not a second copy of it.

areas.label: Trajectory
areas.plain_question: How does today's work move toward that destination?
areas.plain_english: Today's build steps in order, and then a separate, clearly marked explanatory link to the destination. Finishing the last build step does not start the destination work.

anatomy.label: Memory / State
anatomy.what_it_does: Stores decisions, the current build phase, recorded work items and findings in one database, and hands them back the same way to every screen and every agent.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: Eric's stated problem is that models do not remember anything between sessions. This is the part that does.

anatomy.label: Workbench
anatomy.plain_english: The browser application Eric actually uses.
anatomy.what_it_does: Serves the signed-in web interface: conversation, build path, destination architecture and this project map.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: Without it, every answer would require reading the database or the terminal.

anatomy.label: Authentication
anatomy.plain_english: Knowing who is using the Workbench.
anatomy.what_it_does: Signs an individual in through an external identity provider and attaches a role to the session; an address that is not on the allowlist is refused.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: It replaces a shared password, so an action can be attributed to a person rather than to whoever had the password.

anatomy.label: Braingate
anatomy.plain_english: Talking to the system about a project.
anatomy.what_it_does: Carries project conversation to a model and stores the exchange, while refusing every later-stage action.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: It is the first safe slice of the Workbench: conversation is useful on its own and costs nothing irreversible.

anatomy.label: Pipeline / Hermes
anatomy.plain_english: The machinery that runs multi-model work.
anatomy.what_it_does: Starts a run, sends the work to the configured model gateways, collects the draft and the reviews, and records every round.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: It is the checks-and-balances loop: one model drafts, different models review, and the reasoning is kept.

anatomy.label: Recovery
anatomy.plain_english: Being able to explain and rebuild the project's true state from scratch.
anatomy.what_it_does: Assembles the canonical state and a bounded recovery packet an outside reviewer can be handed, and records whether the pushed code has actually been independently checked.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: If a session, a container or a machine is lost, the project has to be recoverable from written evidence rather than from memory.

anatomy.label: Build Visualization
anatomy.plain_english: Seeing where the build is without reading prose.
anatomy.what_it_does: Turns the roadmap row, the decisions and the findings ledger into a diagram and a set of panels.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: The build order previously existed only as long sentences in a database field.

anatomy.label: Dormant Execution Features
anatomy.plain_english: Finished features that are deliberately switched off.
anatomy.what_it_does: Card Factory can draft a work card using a paid model; Card Runner can start a real agent process. Neither is plugged in.
anatomy.why_cis_needs_it: They are the later stages of the Workbench. Keeping them unregistered is how the project guarantees nothing spends money or runs an agent before it is meant to.

capabilities.label: Authentication
capabilities.plain_english: Lets a named person sign in to the Workbench, and refuses anyone not on the list.

capabilities.label: Braingate Conversation
capabilities.plain_english: Allows Eric to talk with Braingate about a project while later execution features remain turned off.

capabilities.label: System Recovery
capabilities.plain_english: Produces one honest description of the project's current state that an outsider can be handed when something has gone wrong.

capabilities.label: Build Path Visualization
capabilities.plain_english: Shows the current build order, where the build is now, and what is blocking it.

capabilities.label: Destination Architecture
capabilities.plain_english: Shows what CIS is ultimately being built to support, kept separate from what is being built now.

capabilities.label: Project Map
capabilities.plain_english: This screen. Explains in plain language how problems, work, capabilities, code, the build order and the destination relate to each other, and says plainly where no connection has been recorded.

capabilities.label: Pipeline Relay
capabilities.plain_english: Runs a piece of work through the draft-and-review loop across several models and records every round.

capabilities.label: Card Factory
capabilities.plain_english: Would draft a work card using a paid model. Deliberately not plugged in: generating costs real money.

capabilities.label: Card Runner
capabilities.plain_english: Would start a real agent process to carry out a card. Deliberately not plugged in: dispatching runs real work on the machine.

capabilities.label: External Developer Verification
capabilities.plain_english: Keeps track of whether an independent reviewer has actually read the pushed code, so finished work is never counted on the author's word alone.

files.plain_english: The main switchboard for the live CIS server.
files.what_it_does: Turns specific backend features on by registering them with Flask.
files.why_it_matters: A capability may exist in code but remain unavailable until this application registers it.
files.technical_role: Flask application entry point for the cis-pipeline container

files.plain_english: The safety wrapper that permits project conversation while blocking later proposal and execution functions.
files.what_it_does: Exposes only the project and message routes, and refuses any request that asks for a downstream action.
files.why_it_matters: The boundary is enforced by which routes exist, not by hiding buttons in the browser.

files.plain_english: The full Workbench backend, including the later stages that are not switched on.
files.what_it_does: Holds the conversation views Braingate reuses, and also the generate and approve routes that are deliberately not registered.
files.why_it_matters: This is why Braingate needed its own wrapper: registering this whole file would switch on paid generation and agent dispatch too.
files.technical_role: Flask Blueprint, NOT registered at this stage

files.plain_english: The sign-in machinery.
files.what_it_does: Runs the login handshake with the external identity provider, issues the session, and reports which Workbench surfaces the server has actually registered.
files.why_it_matters: It answers who is using the Workbench; it never decides which features exist.

files.plain_english: The one place that reads the project's true current state out of the database.
files.what_it_does: Collects the current phase, direction, decisions and open questions, and computes a short fingerprint of that state.
files.why_it_matters: Every other read model shares its database path and its state fingerprint, so two screens cannot disagree about which state they read.

files.plain_english: Builds the bounded packet an outside reviewer is handed when CIS needs diagnosing.
files.what_it_does: Assembles a fixed set of facts about the system into one document.
files.why_it_matters: Recovery has to work when the people who built the thing are not available.

files.plain_english: Works out where the build is by reading the roadmap sentence the project actually recorded.
files.what_it_does: Splits the recorded roadmap into ordered stages, marks the current one, attaches migration unlock points and work items, and lists the findings that block it.
files.why_it_matters: The order is parsed from the database, so the screen cannot carry its own stale copy of the plan.

files.plain_english: Reads the destination architecture out of the decisions that record it.
files.what_it_does: Parses the WIASW node and edge declarations from the ADR-WIASW decision text and reports each one with the sentence it came from.
files.why_it_matters: There is no second stored copy of the architecture, so the picture cannot drift away from the decision.

files.plain_english: Puts the other views together and explains them in plain language.
files.what_it_does: Calls the build path and destination read models rather than repeating them, adds the queue, the findings ledger and a derived capability view, and labels every connection with how well it is evidenced.
files.why_it_matters: It is the only place that says, out loud, where no connection has been recorded.

files.plain_english: The plain-English wording used on the Project Map.
files.what_it_does: Holds reviewed explanations keyed to terms, capabilities, files and findings.
files.why_it_matters: The explanations are written and reviewed in the repository, so no model is asked to invent them while the page loads.

files.plain_english: The single web address the Project Map screen reads from.
files.what_it_does: Hands the composed read model to the browser and nothing else.
files.why_it_matters: One read-only route means the screen has no way to change anything.

files.plain_english: The Project Map screen itself.
files.what_it_does: Draws the six views, the plain-language detail panels and the three levels of detail.
files.why_it_matters: It holds no knowledge of its own: everything it shows arrives in the response.

files.plain_english: The Build Path screen, reused by the Project Map rather than copied into it.
files.what_it_does: Renders the current build panels; the Project Map imports the same panel component.
files.why_it_matters: One renderer means the two screens cannot show different build states.

files.plain_english: The Destination Architecture screen, reused by the Project Map rather than copied into it.
files.what_it_does: Fetches and renders the destination architecture.
files.why_it_matters: The Project Map embeds this component, so there is no second destination view to keep in step.

files.plain_english: The web address that starts and reports on pipeline runs.
files.what_it_does: Accepts a request to start a run and exposes the run's recorded progress.
files.why_it_matters: It is the only blueprint the container registered before the Workbench work began.

files.plain_english: The machinery that actually drives a run through drafting and review.
files.what_it_does: Assembles prompts, calls the model gateways, records each deliberation round.
files.why_it_matters: It is the layer that keeps model-specific detail out of the user interface.

files.plain_english: Would draft a work card with a paid model. Not switched on.
files.what_it_does: Exposes a generate route that spends real money when registered.
files.why_it_matters: Its absence from the switchboard is the guarantee that nothing is being spent.

files.plain_english: Would start a real agent process to carry out a card. Not switched on.
files.what_it_does: Exposes a dispatch route that spawns an agent subprocess when registered.
files.why_it_matters: Its absence from the switchboard is the guarantee that no agent is being launched.

files.plain_english: The write-once record of what happened during development work.
files.what_it_does: Appends numbered events — proposals, decisions, findings, reconciliations — for a task.
files.why_it_matters: Findings cannot be silently edited away; a finding is closed by adding a reconciliation, not by deleting it.

files.plain_english: Decides which recorded findings still count as open.
files.what_it_does: Reads the ledger and reports each finding's disposition and whether a reconciliation has closed it.
files.why_it_matters: The same rule is used by the closeout gate and by these screens, so they cannot disagree.

discoveries.plain_english: Braingate cannot currently get a real response from DeepSeek.
discoveries.why_it_matters: The conversation feature is turned on, but its configured model credential is rejected, so a signed-in user sees an error message where the answer should be. Only Eric can replace the key.

discoveries.plain_english: A failed model call used to be saved as if it were a real reply.
discoveries.why_it_matters: A stored error string looked identical to a genuine answer in the conversation history. Fixed: the code now fails honestly instead of writing a fake turn.

discoveries.plain_english: The public web address pointed at the wrong server, so Braingate was live but unreachable.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Signing in at the public address gave the interface but no conversation. Fixed: the tunnel now points at the real production listener.

discoveries.plain_english: The generated project briefing file is close to its hard size limit.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Ordinary updates to the recorded state can push it over the limit, which breaks the pre-commit export and shows up as an unrelated-looking test failure.

discoveries.plain_english: An obsolete background service keeps crashing and restarting forever.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Nothing depends on it, but anyone checking service health sees a failing CIS service next to the healthy ones and draws the wrong conclusion.

discoveries.plain_english: A background program constantly rewrites a tracked log file, so the repository is never clean.
discoveries.why_it_matters: A careless commit would sweep a few hundred thousand machine-written lines into unrelated work, and the permanent noise hides real uncommitted changes.

discoveries.plain_english: The automatic pre-commit step was unsafe to run.
discoveries.why_it_matters: It would have quietly added unrelated generated files to a narrow commit. Fixed.

discoveries.plain_english: A superseded web service unit is crash-looping.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Not user-facing, but it burns restarts and fills the system log.

discoveries.plain_english: A live API key was committed into the repository and has not been rotated.
discoveries.why_it_matters: The key must be treated as exposed: revoked and replaced first, then removed from the file and from history in its own piece of work.

discoveries.plain_english: The browser asked for a feature the server had not switched on, and showed a confusing error.
discoveries.why_it_matters: The security boundary held — the route genuinely did not exist — but the message read like a breakage rather than a stage that has not been reached. Fixed.

discoveries.plain_english: The public tunnel has no automatic restart policy.
discoveries.why_it_matters: If it crashes, every CIS public address goes off the internet until a person notices.

discoveries.plain_english: The website does not force secure connections.
discoveries.why_it_matters: A mistyped address could serve the application unencrypted. The session cookie is already protected, so the impact is limited, but it should be switched on before real use.

discoveries.plain_english: The development origin is a hand-started program that does not survive a reboot.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Acceptable for development, and deliberately not fixed, because the real registered surface replaces it.

discoveries.plain_english: The roadmap names three work items only in prose; nothing in the database links them.
discoveries.why_it_matters: If triage renumbers or merges those items, the roadmap's references break silently and nothing reports it.

discoveries.plain_english: An old synchronization tool can silently move the recorded build state backwards.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Running it would overwrite the current phase and next action with content from a retired plan, with no error. The standing instruction is: do not run it.

discoveries.plain_english: The work list and the build order classify work on different axes, and triage has to reconcile them.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Labelling items without deciding how the two framings fit together would mis-scope work or quietly drop a distinction the list depends on.

discoveries.plain_english: The Destination Architecture page is in the repository but answers an error on the running server until it restarts.
discoveries.why_it_matters: Opening the tab on the live Workbench looks like a broken feature when it is really a stale process.

discoveries.plain_english: The real external sign-in proof needs a person with a browser.
discoveries.why_it_matters: It cannot be completed by an agent, so it stays open until Eric does it.

queue_items.plain_english: Before any gate is allowed to block work, there has to be a proven way to switch it off from outside.
queue_items.why_it_matters: An earlier version deadlocked because the only way to clear a gate was something the gate itself could prevent you from doing.

queue_items.plain_english: Turning on the automatic guardrails needs an override policy that does not exist yet.
queue_items.why_it_matters: A real run showed a guardrail failing the work and being right to. Without a policy for overriding it, arming the guardrails could stop legitimate work with no way through.

queue_items.plain_english: A run that actually writes code has never completed from start to finish.
queue_items.why_it_matters: The pipeline has been proved on a documentation task, where every code-checking step skipped itself. This is the real end-to-end proof the build is aiming at.
